# 2. Technologies Worth Watching

---

**Technology:** Zimbra Collaboration Suite Actively-Exploited RCE (CVE-2026-73570)

**Category:** Enterprise Solutions / Security / Cloud & Infrastructure

**What happened?** An OS command-injection flaw (CVSS 8.9) in Zimbra Collaboration Suite versions before 10.1.20 lets an unauthenticated attacker send crafted SMTP requests to execute arbitrary OS commands as the Zimbra user, when the optional `zimbra-snmp` package is installed with SNMP notifications enabled. CERT Polska reported active exploitation on August 17; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on August 21 with a federal remediation deadline of **today, August 24**. Shadowserver counts roughly 12,100 internet-exposed Zimbra servers, concentrated in Europe and Asia.

**Why it matters?** Zimbra is a common on-premises email/collaboration platform for mid-size organizations seeking an alternative to Exchange, and unauthenticated RCE on a mail server is a high-value beachhead for an attacker (mail access, lateral movement, credential harvesting). This extends the "actively-exploited unpatched infrastructure" pattern this office has tracked since early August into on-premises email/collaboration, a layer not previously hit this month.

**Business Value:** If Zimbra Collaboration Suite is in use, upgrade to 10.1.20+ immediately, or — if immediate patching isn't possible — disable the `zimbra-snmp` package and SNMP notifications as an interim mitigation. Low effort, high value given the active-exploitation status and today's deadline.

**Company Relevance:** 35 (materially higher if Zimbra is the company's mail/collaboration platform; near-zero otherwise)

**Priority:** High (if applicable)

**Recommendation:** Adopt (immediate patch/mitigation verification)

**Expected Impact:** Short

**Technology:** Nvidia Warns of >15% AI Server Price Hikes on 2027 Shipments (DRAM/HBM Supply Crunch)

**Category:** Cloud & Infrastructure / Artificial Intelligence / Global Technology Companies

**What happened?** Nvidia notified its largest customers, and the contract manufacturers building AI servers for Microsoft, Google, and Oracle, that AI server prices will rise more than 15% on systems shipping in early 2027, spanning both the Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell platforms. The root cause is a DRAM/HBM supply crunch: memory makers (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) are redirecting fab capacity toward AI-grade memory, and commodity DDR5 pricing is reportedly up roughly 485% year-over-year as a knock-on effect. First reported by Bloomberg on August 22, with follow-on analysis through August 23.

**Why it matters?** This is a specific, quantified, forward-dated cost signal — not a vague "AI costs are rising" observation — and it lands on top of, and compounds, the Samsung foundry price hikes already flagged in the prior edition. Server lead times mean 2027 capacity commitments are effectively being priced now; any company with GPU/cloud-capacity plans extending into 2027, whether direct hardware purchases or reserved cloud instances, is exposed to this cost pressure, and cloud providers are likely to pass at least part of it through in on-demand/reserved GPU pricing.

**Business Value:** Flag this to whoever owns 2027 infrastructure or cloud-compute budget planning now, before commitments are locked in. No immediate spend decision is required, but budget models assuming flat or declining AI-compute costs into 2027 should be revised to reflect confirmed upside risk.

**Company Relevance:** 40 (higher for any team planning GPU capacity, on-prem AI infrastructure, or large reserved cloud-compute commitments into 2027)

**Priority:** Medium

**Recommendation:** Observe (update budget assumptions; no purchasing action implied)

**Expected Impact:** Medium-Long

**Technology:** Anthropic Hires Ex-Google TPU Chief Amir Salek for Its Compute/Silicon Effort

**Category:** Artificial Intelligence / Cloud & Infrastructure / Global Technology Companies

**What happened?** Anthropic hired Amir Salek — who led Google's custom TPU silicon program through seven generations, most recently at Cerberus Capital — to join its compute team, reporting to compute lead James Bradbury. Reported by Bloomberg on August 21.

**Why it matters?** This is the clearest evidence yet that Anthropic's custom-silicon ambitions are a led initiative with proven, hyperscaler-caliber chip-architecture leadership, not just a stated long-term intent. # 3. New Tools & Platforms

**Tool:** GitHub Copilot CLI v1.0.81-8

**What does it do?** Shipped August 23, this release adds "xhigh" reasoning-effort support for Grok 4.6, makes path-sourced plugins in local marketplaces load live from their real directory (no `/plugin update` needed), and fixes a bug where signing out failed to clear cached enterprise-managed settings — meaning a user who signed back in was getting a stale policy instead of a freshly fetched one.

**Who should use it?** Any team using GitHub Copilot CLI, particularly organizations enforcing Copilot governance via enterprise-managed settings.

**Business Use Case:** The sign-out/policy-caching fix closes a small but real compliance gap — a user who previously signed out and back in may have been operating under an outdated managed policy without anyone noticing.

**Estimated ROI:** High if applicable — a routine update with no adoption cost that closes a real (if narrow) governance gap.

**Recommended Experiment:** Not applicable — confirm the Copilot CLI fleet is on v1.0.81-8 or later if enterprise-managed settings are enforced.

# 4. Global Technology Direction

**Where is the market moving?**

Two threads this window sharpen patterns already tracked rather than introducing new ones.

**First, AI hardware costs are now confirmed to be turning upward across every layer of the supply chain simultaneously, not just at the foundry level.** The prior edition flagged Samsung's foundry price hikes as the first sign of AI-driven pricing power reversing a years-long downward trend. This window supplies the finished-server-layer confirmation: Nvidia is warning its largest customers of a >15% price increase on 2027 shipments, driven by a DRAM/HBM supply crunch as memory makers redirect capacity toward AI-grade parts. Foundry pricing, memory pricing, and now finished-server pricing are moving in the same direction at the same time — this is no longer an isolated data point but a stack-wide cost trend.

**Second, both sovereign compute buildout and frontier-lab custom-silicon efforts are deepening in parallel.** Nvidia's "FRONTia" partnership with Japan's METI extends the state-backed AI-infrastructure financing pattern (previously seen in Ohio/SB Energy) into a new G7 geography, while Anthropic's hire of a veteran Google TPU architect shows frontier labs' custom-silicon ambitions are moving from stated intent to led initiatives with real chip-architecture leadership. Both point toward a multi-year restructuring of who controls AI compute supply and at what cost — hyperscalers and governments building dedicated capacity, and frontier labs working to reduce single-supplier (Nvidia) dependency.

**What This Means For Our Company**

Treat AI infrastructure and cloud-compute cost assumptions for 2027 as having confirmed upside risk across foundry, memory, and finished-server layers — this should be an explicit, dated input to any budget model extending into next year, not a vague caveat. On vendor dependency, continue folding new data points (this window: Anthropic's TPU hire; prior window: its IPO process and compute financing) into the lightweight AI-vendor-concentration review already flagged as in-progress in recent editions, so it stays current rather than needing to be rebuilt from scratch when a forcing event (e.g., an S-1 filing) arrives.
